Chapter 5: Habits in Organizations—How Group Routines Drive Success or Failure
You know, habits aren’t just something we deal with on a personal level. They actually play a huge role in how groups, teams, and entire organizations operate. In fact, those routines you see at work or in any group setting? They’re really just shared habits that guide everyone’s behavior—even when nobody’s spelling out the rules.
Think about it: over time, as groups try to solve problems or hit their goals, they naturally come up with ways of doing things. Maybe it’s the way you all start meetings, or how your team handles customer complaints. These routines become the go-to way of working, and before you know it, they’re shaping your workplace culture and performance.
The real power behind these organizational habits is how they help everyone coordinate and keep things consistent. Take a hospital, for example. If nurses and doctors get into the habit of double-checking medications, errors drop and patients are safer. Or imagine a retail store where every employee greets you with a smile—suddenly, shopping there just feels a little better, and sales go up.
But here’s something to pay attention to—sometimes, these group routines stick around even when they’re not helping anymore. Maybe they’re just comfortable, or nobody questions them. And that can get in the way of progress. If you want to change things, you really have to dig in and figure out what cues, routines, and rewards are keeping those old habits alive.
That’s where leaders come in. They’re in a unique spot to spot what’s working—and what’s not. By zeroing in on what’s called “keystone habits”—those routines that kind of set the tone for everything else—leaders can spark changes that ripple throughout the organization. For instance, a manager who makes open communication the norm can end up boosting trust and teamwork across the whole group.
So, how do you actually make change stick in an organization? It usually follows a few clear steps:
First, diagnose the current habits. Really watch how people work together day to day.
Next, find those keystone habits—the ones that have the biggest impact.
Then, design new routines that match up with your goals.
And finally, reinforce those new habits with rewards, recognition, and a little social encouragement to help them last.
Social dynamics matter a lot here. When influential people or leaders start doing something new, others usually follow. It creates this shared sense of purpose and helps change really take root.
At the end of the day, organizational habits are powerful because they shape how groups act, react, and grow together. If you can spot these routines and intentionally guide them, you’ll help your organization perform better, adapt to new challenges, and build a culture where improvement just comes naturally.
